A browser asks for a resource, and a server answers with a status, headers and content. Follow a page request from the first name lookup to the HTML that arrives at your screen. Each packet can be paused, opened and read one byte at a time.

DNS found the address and TCP opened an ordered connection. HTTP carried the request and HTML reply. The browser can now parse the page and fetch its other resources. Replay to trace each packet again.

The browser splits the address into its host name and path. It first needs the server's IP address, then a TCP connection. The request will ask for the root page. HTTP can send its message once those lower layers are ready.

The client asks its resolver for the IPv4 address of www.example.com. A reply associates that name with 203.0.113.10 so the browser can address its connection. Cached records avoid another lookup. Each reply has a time to live that limits reuse.
A SYN proposes the client's first sequence number. The server returns SYN-ACK, and the client sends ACK. Both ends can now track an ordered stream of bytes.

The browser sends GET / to request the root document. The server answers with 200 OK and an HTML body. TCP splits that body across nine segments; the receiver puts their bytes back in order for the browser.
The browser parses the returned HTML into a document tree. It lays out the elements and paints the page. References to images or stylesheets would trigger more requests.
HTTPS places HTTP inside an authenticated encrypted connection. The browser still resolves a name and opens TCP, but TLS protects the request and response from observers along the path.

DNS found the address and TCP opened the stream. TLS authenticated the server and established traffic keys before HTTP sent the page request. The browser received and decrypted the response locally, leaving observers with encrypted records rather than the page contents.
The https scheme asks the browser to use TLS before sending HTTP. The host name also identifies the service whose certificate must be checked.
Same lookup as HTTP, not encrypted
The client resolves www.example.com to an IPv4 address. Encryption of the later HTTP exchange does not by itself encrypt a conventional UDP DNS lookup.
A three-way handshake establishes TCP state at both endpoints. Port 443 selects the HTTPS service, while the client uses an ephemeral port.
Agrees on keys, checks the certificate

The client offers a TLS version, cipher suites and a key share. The server selects compatible parameters and proves its identity through a certificate and signature. Both sides confirm the handshake before ordinary application data.
The browser’s GET request is encrypted before it enters TCP. The server encrypts the response too. A packet observer can see endpoints and record sizes, but cannot read the HTTP content.
TLS authenticates and decrypts received records locally. The browser then interprets the HTTP response and renders the HTML, just as it would after an unencrypted HTTP transfer.
WebSocket turns an HTTP connection into a lasting channel for messages in both directions. Follow the upgrade, exchange live data, and close the channel cleanly.
The peers negotiated a message channel over a reliable byte stream. They exchanged application messages and control frames before closing the connection.
TCP to the server, as for HTTP
The browser first opens a TCP connection to the server. WebSocket needs that ordered byte stream before its HTTP upgrade can begin.
An HTTP request with Upgrade: websocket
An HTTP request asks the server to switch protocols. A fresh challenge key lets the browser check that the response belongs to this upgrade.
The server accepts with status 101 and a derived accept value. Both endpoints now interpret subsequent bytes as WebSocket frames.
SHA-1 of the key + a fixed string
Either endpoint can send a message without waiting for a new HTTP request. Client frames are masked, and frame boundaries preserve message structure.
A ping asks whether the peer is still responsive. The matching pong keeps application liveness separate from the underlying TCP connection.
A close frame communicates the reason for ending the channel. The other endpoint acknowledges it before the transport is released.

WebRTC combines signaling, connectivity checks and media encryption to connect browsers. Trace candidate discovery, ICE path selection and DTLS key establishment before protected audio and video flow.
Introduced by a server, then direct

Signaling exchanged session descriptions, ICE selected a reachable path and DTLS established media keys. Protected media then used that path, with a relay available when direct connectivity was impossible.
The browser joins an application’s signaling session. Signaling exchanges setup information but does not have to carry the eventual media stream.
A STUN request discovers the address and port observed outside the local NAT. That mapped address becomes one of the connectivity candidates.
An SDP description, via the server
An offer describes supported media, codecs and connectivity credentials. It also identifies certificate fingerprints used to authenticate the later DTLS exchange.
The other browser returns compatible session parameters and its candidates. Both peers now have enough information to attempt connectivity checks.
ICE checks candidate pairs using authenticated STUN messages. Successful checks identify a path that can carry traffic through the relevant NAT mappings.
The selected peers negotiate DTLS and verify the signaled certificate fingerprints. Keying material from that handshake protects the media session.
Audio and video use protected RTP packets with independent sequence and media timestamps. Arrival time can vary without changing the intended media timeline.
A successful direct path avoids sending every media packet through the signaling server. If direct checks fail, a TURN relay can provide a reachable alternative.
QUIC combines secure connection setup and reliable streams over UDP. Follow an HTTP/3 exchange and see how a connection identifier can survive a network-address change.
One round trip, then the request
QUIC protected independent application streams without relying on a TCP connection. Connection identifiers allowed the session to continue when the outer network path changed.
An earlier visit said it can
The client chooses HTTP/3 for the requested origin. QUIC will carry the HTTP exchange over UDP rather than first opening a TCP byte stream.
Initial packets begin TLS negotiation and advertise connection identifiers. Packet padding and protection follow QUIC’s rules even before final application keys exist.
The server returns its selected parameters and encrypted handshake flight. Multiple datagrams can carry certificate data while packet acknowledgments track delivery.
The request, one round trip in
The client finishes authenticating the handshake and sends its HTTP request. QUIC streams provide ordering within a stream without making every stream wait behind unrelated data.
The server returns the HTTP response on the chosen stream. QUIC packet numbers and stream offsets serve different roles in delivery and reassembly.
All but a few header bits
Known by ID, not by address
A new network can change the client’s address or port. Connection identifiers and path validation let an existing connection move to that path safely.
TCP gives applications an ordered byte stream. Sequence numbers, acknowledgments and retransmission let it recover from loss without asking the application to assemble packets itself.

The receiver buffered later data while a missing range held back delivery. Duplicate acknowledgments and a SACK block identified that hole. Retransmitting the missing 100 bytes let the receiver acknowledge the complete 300-byte stream before both sides closed.
The client sends SYN and the server responds with SYN-ACK. A final ACK completes the handshake. Each side now knows the other side’s initial sequence position.
The first segment carries bytes 1 through 100. The receiver acknowledges 101, meaning it now expects that byte next.

The sender transmits two more ranges of the stream. The middle range is lost, while the later range reaches the receiver. TCP can buffer that later data without presenting an incomplete stream to the application.

The receiver keeps acknowledging 101 because that byte has not arrived. A selective acknowledgment reports the later range it already has. The sender can distinguish the missing data from buffered data.
The sender retransmits the missing range. Once it arrives, the receiver can advance its cumulative acknowledgment past all three ranges and release the contiguous stream.
A FIN says the sender has no more stream data. Both directions are acknowledged and closed independently. The endpoints then release their connection state after the appropriate closing period.
UDP sends individual messages without a transport handshake. It preserves datagram boundaries but leaves recovery, ordering and timing decisions to the application.

Voice frames left without a transport handshake. One datagram was lost, but subsequent frames continued on schedule. RTP supplied ordering and timing information, while the application chose how to handle the missing audio.
The first 0.2 s of a call
The first voice frame can leave immediately. UDP adds source and destination ports, a length and a checksum, without establishing a TCP-style connection.
One every 20 ms, each on its own
The sender encodes small pieces of audio into separate datagrams. RTP sequence numbers and timestamps describe their order and playback timing. UDP itself does not interpret those media fields.
One datagram fails to reach the receiver. UDP has no automatic retransmission, so the next voice frame continues on schedule. The receiver notices the gap through the RTP sequence number.
The remote endpoint sends voice frames back to the client’s port. These are independent messages rather than TCP acknowledgments. The application manages the two media streams.
Reliability is up to the app

A voice application may conceal the missing sound rather than wait for a late retransmission. A different UDP application could implement its own reliable delivery. UDP leaves that policy above the transport layer.
IP addresses packets and forwards them between networks. Routers select the next hop using the destination address; the link-layer envelope changes at each hop while IP spans the route.

ARP found the gateway’s local MAC address, and an Ethernet frame carried a remotely addressed IP datagram to that gateway. Routers forwarded it toward the destination while reducing TTL. The capture remained on the home network, before outbound NAT and after reverse translation of the reply.
Compare the address with the subnet

The client compares its subnet with the destination address. 203.0.113.10 is outside 192.168.1.0/24, so the default route points to 192.168.1.1. The server’s IP stays the destination even though the first link goes to the router.
ARP turns an IP into a MAC
The laptop broadcasts an ARP request for the gateway’s local address. The router answers with its MAC address. ARP does not discover the remote web server’s MAC across the Internet.

The Ethernet destination is the router, while the IPv4 destination is the web server. The laptop sends the encapsulated packet on the local link. The router removes that link envelope before forwarding it.

A typical home router translates the client’s private source address and records a mapping. Every router along the route also decrements TTL and chooses a next hop. This capture is taken before NAT, so it retains the client’s private address.
NAT translates it for the laptop
The response follows routes toward the translated address. The home router uses its mapping to deliver it to 192.168.1.10. The local capture shows that packet after reverse translation.
BGP exchanges reachability between autonomous systems. Follow session establishment, route advertisement and withdrawal, then connect routing policy to the packets that follow it.
BGP distributed route information rather than carrying the application’s data. Policy and path attributes determined the selected next hop, while a withdrawal removed obsolete reachability.
The internet consists of networks operated under different routing policies. BGP lets those autonomous systems advertise which prefixes they can reach.
Two routers open a TCP session for BGP. The reliable transport carries routing messages independently of later user traffic.
OPEN messages identify the speakers and advertise capabilities. KEEPALIVE messages confirm that the session remains responsive.
An UPDATE advertises a reachable prefix and its path attributes. The receiving router applies policy before accepting or selecting that route.
A router can advertise an accepted route to another peer under its export policy. The AS path records network traversal and helps prevent loops.
Application packets follow the installed forwarding route. Their path depends on routing decisions, but they do not travel inside BGP messages.
A withdrawal removes a previously advertised route. Peers must select another usable path or stop forwarding toward that destination.
A route announcement is not automatically proof of address ownership. Origin validation and operational policy reduce the impact of incorrect or malicious announcements.
An IPv6 host can configure itself using local discovery and router advertisements. Watch duplicate-address detection, prefix discovery and neighbour lookup prepare the host for communication.
The host obtained a usable address and learned its router’s link address without an IPv4 ARP exchange. IPv6 neighbour discovery carried these local configuration messages.
The host forms a link-local IPv6 address for communication on this network. Duplicate-address detection checks whether another interface already claims it.
A router solicitation asks local routers to advertise their configuration. Its multicast destination reaches the devices responsible for this link.
Prefix, MTU and DNS in one message
A router advertisement supplies a prefix, routing lifetime and other settings. The host uses those values according to the advertised configuration flags.
The host forms a global address from the advertised prefix and its interface identifier. It tests that address before treating it as usable.
Neighbour solicitation resolves the next-hop IPv6 address to a link address. A neighbour advertisement provides the mapping used for local frame delivery.
The address and route are now ready for ordinary traffic. DHCPv6 may supply additional configuration in other networks, but this exchange did not require it.
DNS connects readable names with resource records. A recursive resolver can follow the naming hierarchy, cache what it learns and return a result to the client.

The recursive resolver followed the root, top-level domain and authoritative server to obtain the requested address. It returned that answer to the client and cached it for the record’s lifetime. A later lookup can reuse valid cached data instead of repeating every exchange.
The laptop hands the question off

The laptop asks its recursive resolver for www.example.com. If no usable cached answer exists, the resolver continues on the client’s behalf. The client does not normally contact each authority itself.

The resolver asks a root server where to continue. The root points toward the top-level domain’s name servers rather than returning the final web address. Referrals reduce the problem one delegation at a time.
The resolver contacts a .com server next. That server identifies the authority for the example domain. The resolver can cache delegation information as well as final answers.
The authoritative server holds the domain’s published records. It returns an A record associating www.example.com with 203.0.113.10. This completes the resolver’s search for the requested address.

The resolver returns the address to the laptop and caches it for its remaining TTL. Later queries can avoid the full hierarchy while the record remains valid. A DNS TTL is a cache lifetime, separate from the hop-limiting IPv4 TTL.
DNS over HTTPS carries DNS messages inside an authenticated web connection. Compare the visible plaintext lookup with a protected lookup, while separating privacy from the resolver’s trustworthiness.
HTTPS concealed the DNS message from observers on the path. The selected resolver still processed the question, and connection metadata remained visible outside encryption.
The site’s address you then visit
Can’t be changed on the way
Readable by anyone on the way
A conventional DNS message exposes its question to observers along the path. The reply also reveals the returned records and their cache lifetimes.
The client establishes an authenticated HTTPS connection to its configured resolver. Bootstrap information must already tell it how to reach that service.
A DNS message in an HTTP request
The DNS question is encoded inside the HTTPS application exchange. Network observers can see the connection but cannot read the protected query contents.
The DNS answer in an HTTP response
The resolver returns a DNS response inside the protected connection. The client decodes the DNS records after HTTPS authentication and decryption.
Hidden on the way, not from the resolver
Encryption does not hide the resolver endpoint, traffic timing or every destination signal. The resolver itself still sees the names it is asked to resolve.
The site’s IP, maybe its name
DNSSEC adds signatures and a chain of trust to DNS data. Follow an answer’s signature through zone keys and parent delegations to a configured trust anchor.
A chain of signatures to the root
Validation connected the answer’s signature to trusted key material. DNSSEC authenticates DNS data; it does not encrypt the question or its response.
The client asks its resolver for the desired DNS record. A validating resolver can request the signatures needed to check the returned data.
An RRSIG comes with the A record
The answer arrives with a signature covering its record set. The signature must be checked against an appropriate zone key and its validity period.
The resolver obtains the zone’s DNSKEY records. A valid signature alone is insufficient until the key’s authority is established.
The parent zone supplies a DS record identifying the child’s trusted key. The resolver checks that delegation against the signed child key material.
Validation follows signed delegations toward a configured trust anchor. A break in this chain prevents treating the response as securely authenticated.
The resolver returns a validated result when all required checks succeed. A validation failure is different from an ordinary unsigned answer.
DHCP supplies an address lease and the network settings a host needs. A client discovers a server, selects an offer and receives confirmation before using the configuration.
Leased, and kept up to date

Discover, Offer, Request and Acknowledge established the client’s lease. The configuration included a router and DNS resolver as well as an address. A later unicast renewal extended the lease without repeating the initial broadcast discovery.
A new client knows its link-layer identity but lacks usable IPv4 settings. It cannot yet use the normal default gateway or resolver. DHCP bootstraps that configuration on the local network.
The client broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER so a local server can hear it. UDP ports 68 and 67 identify client and server. A transaction ID lets everyone recognize replies to this negotiation.
The server offers 192.168.1.10 for a limited lifetime. Options describe the subnet, gateway and DNS resolver. An offer is a proposal, not yet the client’s final authorization to use the address.

The client requests the offered address and identifies the chosen server. Broadcasting this selection also tells other DHCP servers that their offers were not selected. The address is still subject to the server’s confirmation.
DHCPACK confirms the lease and repeats the settings. After checking that the address is safe to use, the client configures its interface. It can now contact the gateway and resolve names.

At the renewal time, the configured client normally unicasts DHCPREQUEST to its server. An ACK extends the lease. If renewal fails for long enough, the client must eventually stop using the expired address.
ICMP reports network conditions and supports diagnostic probes. Ping measures replies, while traceroute uses expiring hop limits to reveal responding routers along a path.

An echo exchange tested the destination and supplied a round-trip measurement. Probes with increasing TTL illustrated how traceroute discovers responding hops. A port-unreachable reply showed that a packet can reach a host even when no application accepts its destination port.

The client sends an ICMP Echo Request to the server. An identifier and sequence number distinguish the probe. A reply can demonstrate reachability, though a missing reply alone does not prove the host is down.

The destination returns an Echo Reply containing the original echo data. The sender matches its identifier and sequence number, then measures elapsed time. This is a round-trip measurement rather than one-way latency.
A traceroute probe starts with TTL 1. The home router decrements it to zero and discards the packet. An ICMP Time Exceeded message quotes the beginning of that original datagram.
The next probe has a larger TTL and can travel farther. The next responding hop sends its own Time Exceeded message. Real paths may have nonresponding hops or change between probes.
Increasing TTL step by step reveals a sequence of responding hops. Each response measures a separate round trip from the client. It does not guarantee that every packet takes an identical path.

A UDP probe can reach the destination but find no application listening on its port. The host may answer with ICMP Destination Unreachable, code 3. Traditional UDP traceroute uses that reply as its destination signal.
Network Time Protocol estimates clock offset despite transit delay. Follow the four timestamps in a request and reply, then see why a system normally adjusts its clock gradually.
The client used both directions of the exchange to estimate delay and offset. Multiple samples and careful clock adjustment reduce the impact of jitter and sudden clock jumps.
The laptop’s clock is a little slow
Independent clocks drift because their oscillators are imperfect. A client periodically compares its clock with a selected time source.
The request records the client’s transmit time. The server will echo that value so the reply can be matched to this particular sample.
T2 and T3 from the server, T4 on arrival
The server includes its receive and transmit timestamps. The client adds its local arrival time to complete the four-timestamp observation.
The client estimates transit delay and clock offset from the four timestamps. The estimate assumes that the two directions have roughly comparable delay.
A clock discipline process combines repeated samples and adjusts the local clock. Gradual slewing avoids disruptive jumps while tracking the reference time.
Joining Wi-Fi combines network discovery, association and key establishment. Watch a station find an access point, complete WPA2 key negotiation, and send protected data.
Eleven frames to a secure link
The station discovered the network and established shared encryption keys. Later radio frames protect their payload while leaving enough header information for local delivery.
An access point periodically advertises its network in beacon frames. A station can also probe for networks and read their advertised capabilities.
The station authenticates at the wireless MAC layer and requests association. Association assigns local state, but it does not yet establish data-encryption keys.
The access point supplies a fresh nonce and the station returns its own. Both derive pairwise keys from the shared secret, addresses and these challenges.
The access point proves possession of the derived key and delivers group-key information. The station confirms receipt so protected traffic can begin.
And what a listener could still do
Data frames now carry encrypted payload and integrity protection. The wireless headers still identify radio endpoints and support retransmission.
WPA3 replaces a captured-password guessing opportunity with an interactive password-authenticated exchange. Follow SAE, then see how its result feeds the familiar wireless key handshake.
SAE established a secret without transmitting the password. Association and the four-way handshake then installed the keys used for protected wireless traffic.
The network advertises SAE as its authentication method. The station checks the advertised security capabilities before selecting the access point.
Each side commits to the password
Both peers send fresh scalar and group-element contributions. These values bind the exchange to the password without sending that password over the air.
Each side confirms the shared result with an authenticator. A peer with a different password cannot produce the expected confirmation.
Then the 4-way handshake, as in WPA2
The station associates and completes the four-way key handshake. Fresh nonces turn the SAE result into keys for this specific connection.
An observed SAE transcript does not provide the same offline guessing test as a WPA2 handshake. Strong passwords and correct endpoint implementations still matter.
Enterprise Wi-Fi separates radio access from central identity verification. Follow EAP-TLS through the access point and RADIUS server, then install the wireless session keys.
Its own login, its own keys
The authentication server verified the client and returned an access decision with key material. The access point used that result to establish encryption on the local wireless link.
The access point asks for an identity
The access point asks the station to identify itself through EAP. Association alone does not authorize ordinary traffic on this enterprise network.
The login goes to the server
The access point packages the EAP exchange in a RADIUS request. The authentication server decides which challenge or response should follow.
The server proves who it is
EAP-TLS carries a TLS handshake inside authentication messages. Large TLS records may be fragmented across several EAP or RADIUS messages.
The client supplies its certificate and proves possession of the matching private key. That proof authenticates the endpoint without sending its private key.
Both TLS peers verify the handshake transcript and finish key establishment. Authentication succeeds only when the required identity checks complete.
And a key for the access point
The RADIUS server returns acceptance and protected session key material. Attributes may also select a VLAN or other access policy for this user.
As at home, from a different key
The station and access point complete the four-way handshake. Fresh nonces derive the keys that protect this wireless association.
A central identity system can grant, revoke and audit individual access. Its trust configuration and certificate validation remain essential to the result.
A captive network can provide an address while withholding general internet access. Follow the operating system’s connectivity check, the login redirect, and the change after access is granted.
The portal changed the client’s access policy after the user accepted its terms. Connectivity checks can now receive their expected response instead of another login redirect.
An address, but no way out
The client has joined the local network and received configuration. An IP address alone does not prove that ordinary internet access is allowed.
The operating system requests a known connectivity-check resource. Its expected status or body helps distinguish unrestricted access from an interception page.
The router, posing as the server
The wrong answer gives it away
The network returns a redirect toward its portal. The client opens a limited sign-in view instead of treating that response as the requested internet resource.
The portal page explains the network’s access requirements. Its web resources travel through the access path the network permits before sign-in.
The router lets the laptop out
The user submits the portal form or accepts the terms. The portal associates this action with the client’s current access session.
A new connectivity check gets the expected result. The operating system can leave the captive state and allow normal browsing.
SMTP submits and relays messages using a command-and-reply conversation. A sending server looks up the recipient domain’s mail exchanger, then transfers responsibility to another server.

The client submitted mail over a protected connection, and the sending server looked up a mail exchanger. Server-to-server SMTP used a separate connection and upgraded it with STARTTLS. The final acceptance transferred delivery responsibility; it did not reveal whether the recipient had read the message.
The client opens TCP port 465 and negotiates TLS immediately. Only after that protection is ready does SMTP begin. This submission connection is distinct from server-to-server relay.

The server advertises its SMTP capabilities after EHLO. The user authenticates over the protected connection before submitting mail. The packet view shows encrypted records, while the lesson explains their role.

MAIL FROM and RCPT TO specify the transport envelope. DATA then carries the message headers and body, ending with a dot on its own line. A success reply means this server has accepted responsibility for the message.
The sending server asks DNS for MX records of the recipient domain. MX preference numbers help order the candidate mail servers. The relay then resolves and connects to the selected exchanger.
Mail servers normally relay using port 25. When STARTTLS is available and selected, the connection upgrades to TLS before the mail transfer continues. A new EHLO follows the TLS handshake.

The recipient’s server accepts the relayed message and places it in a mailbox or delivery queue. SMTP acceptance is not evidence that a person has read it. Retrieval protocols handle the later mailbox access.
POP3 provides a compact conversation for listing and retrieving messages. It suits download-oriented clients, with deletion applied only after the session successfully enters its update phase.

The client authenticated, listed the mailbox and retrieved a complete message. DELE marked that message, and a successful QUIT committed the deletion. Omitting DELE would have let the client retain the server copy.
TCP connects to the POP3 service on port 995. TLS is negotiated before credentials or mail commands. The server’s identity must be verified before the client trusts that connection.

The server greets the client and accepts authentication commands inside TLS. A successful response moves the session into the transaction state. Example credentials explain the flow without representing a real account.
STAT returns the message count and total size. LIST can provide individual message numbers and sizes. These numbers identify messages within this POP3 session.
RETR asks for a message by its session number. The server returns its headers and body as a multiline response. Dot-stuffing distinguishes data lines from the terminating dot.
DELE marks a message for deletion during this session. QUIT enters the update phase and commits those marks when successful. A client may instead keep server copies by choosing not to send DELE.
IMAP manages mail stored on the server. Clients select mailboxes, fetch selected content and synchronize flags, allowing multiple devices to work with the same mailbox state.

The client selected INBOX and fetched content by UID while leaving the message on the server. IDLE then allowed the server to announce a mailbox change. This separation of server storage, content retrieval and state updates supports synchronized clients.
The client connects to port 993 and establishes TLS before speaking IMAP. Protection applies to credentials, mailbox metadata and content. The server then sends its protocol greeting.
A tagged command authenticates the user inside TLS. The server repeats that tag in its completion response. Tags let a client associate responses with commands even when unsolicited updates arrive.
SELECT opens INBOX for message operations. The server reports message count, flags and UID validity information. Stable UIDs are more useful for synchronization than sequence numbers that may shift.

The client fetches a message or a selected part of it. BODY.PEEK avoids setting the Seen flag merely by retrieving the data. The message remains on the server unless an explicit removal workflow is used.
The client enters IDLE to receive mailbox changes without repeated polling. A server update can announce a new message. DONE ends IDLE so the client can issue further commands.
FTP separates its command conversation from file data. A control connection coordinates authentication and transfer setup, while a second connection carries the selected file.

FTP kept its commands on port 21 and negotiated a passive data port for the file. The data stream closed when the transfer ended, while the control stream reported success and handled QUIT. Both streams were visible in this plain FTP example.
The client opens TCP port 21 for FTP control messages. The server’s 220 greeting indicates that it is ready for a session. This connection will coordinate the later data transfer.
USER and PASS, readable by anyone
USER and PASS authenticate the session. In this plain FTP example, both commands are readable on the wire. A protected protocol is needed when credentials must be confidential.
The server names a data port

PASV asks the server to listen on a separate port. Its reply encodes an address and two port octets. The client initiates the data connection, which usually works more easily through a client-side firewall.

The client connects to the advertised data port and requests a file on the control connection. The server can now deliver file bytes independently of its status replies. The two TCP streams have different endpoint ports.

File contents arrive on the data connection. Closing that stream signals the end of this transfer, and a control reply confirms success. Another file may use a new data connection while the control session stays open.
QUIT ends the FTP session after transfers are complete. The server responds before closing the control connection. Neither of the two plain FTP streams provides encryption by itself.
SMB exposes remote files through authenticated network shares. Trace negotiation, authentication, share connection, and the open/read/close operations used to fetch a file.
The client authenticated a session, connected a share and used a file handle for its operations. Closing the handle releases file state while the larger session may remain available.
A TCP connection to the NAS
The client opens a TCP connection to the file server’s SMB service. File operations will share this transport connection.
The peers select a compatible SMB dialect and security capabilities. Negotiated limits bound later read and write operations.
The NAS sends a random number
Session setup begins a challenge-response authentication exchange. The server’s challenge helps distinguish this attempt from a replay.
The client returns an authentication response derived from its credentials. The server accepts or rejects the session before granting share access.
A tree-connect request identifies the desired network share. The returned tree identifier scopes subsequent operations to that share.
The client requests a file open with explicit access and sharing requirements. The server returns a file identifier for later reads and closure.
The whole file in one request
The client requests bytes at a chosen file offset. The response carries the data and reports how much was returned.
A close request releases the open file handle. Session and transport resources can remain open for later operations.
SSH authenticates a remote host and protects interactive sessions. Its transport negotiates algorithms and keys before user authentication and logical channels are carried inside encrypted packets.
Encrypted from the key exchange on

SSH exchanged banners, negotiated algorithms and authenticated the host during key exchange. The client then proved its user identity without sending its private key. Session channels carried encrypted input and output inside the established transport.
TCP connects to port 22, then both peers exchange SSH version banners. These identification lines are initially readable. They help the peers choose a compatible SSH transport.

Each peer sends KEXINIT with supported key-exchange, host-key and encryption algorithms. Compatible choices are selected from these lists. Negotiating an algorithm is separate from authenticating the host’s identity.
Shared keys, and a host key check

Ephemeral public keys support agreement on shared secret material. The server signs the exchange with its host key, which the client checks against a trusted identity. NEWKEYS switches subsequent packets to the negotiated protection.
The client requests user authentication over the protected transport. A signature proves control of an authorized private key. The private key itself stays on the client.

The client opens a session channel inside the SSH connection. It may request a terminal and an interactive shell. Channel identifiers and flow-control windows let several activities share the protected transport.

Input travels as channel data and the remote process returns its output on that channel. Observers see encrypted packets rather than the command text. Closing the channel need not immediately close every other activity on the SSH connection.

TLS protects application data with authenticated encryption. A handshake negotiates parameters, authenticates the server and derives traffic keys; subsequent records hide their content from the network.
One round trip to set up

The hellos selected TLS 1.3 parameters and exchanged ephemeral public keys. Certificate verification and Finished messages bound the connection to an identity and the handshake transcript. Authenticated encryption then protected application records until the closing alerts.

The client offers supported TLS versions, cipher suites and a public key share. A server-name extension identifies the requested virtual host in this example. The ClientHello is visible here because encrypted client hello is not being used.
The server selects TLS 1.3 and a mutually supported cipher suite. Its key share lets both sides derive handshake protection keys. Messages after ServerHello are generally encrypted in TLS 1.3.

The encrypted handshake includes the certificate chain and a proof using its private key. The client checks the chain, host name and applicable validity rules. A certificate is useful only when those checks connect it to a trusted identity.

Finished authenticates the accumulated handshake messages using derived key material. Both endpoints verify this confirmation. A transcript mismatch prevents the connection from being treated as successfully established.

Application data is sealed into TLS records with authenticated encryption. An authentication tag lets the receiver reject altered data. The packet inspector marks protected content as unknown instead of inventing plaintext bytes.
A close_notify alert indicates that an endpoint has finished sending TLS records. In TLS 1.3 it is protected like other post-handshake content. TCP then handles the underlying stream shutdown.
Forward proxy, and CONNECT for HTTPS
A forward proxy makes requests on a client’s behalf. Compare an ordinary proxied HTTP request with CONNECT, which creates a byte tunnel for an end-to-end TLS connection.
The proxy fetched cleartext HTTP resources directly and relayed protected HTTPS bytes through a tunnel. The location of TLS endpoints determines what content the proxy can read.
The client is configured to use a proxy for web access. This changes the first connection destination without changing the resource the user requested.
The client opens a transport connection to the proxy. The origin server is not the peer of this first TCP connection.
The HTTP request names the full target URL. The proxy needs that authority and path to decide where to forward the request.
Its own connection to the server
The proxy opens its own connection toward the origin. It forwards the request using a separate transport conversation.
The origin’s response returns through the proxy. The proxy relays the status, headers and body to the waiting client.
For HTTPS, the client asks the proxy to CONNECT to a host and port. A successful response changes the connection into a transparent byte tunnel.
The client negotiates TLS with the origin through that tunnel. The proxy can observe connection metadata but cannot read correctly protected application content.
SOCKS5 relays transport connections without requiring the client’s application to speak HTTP. Follow method selection, destination addressing, and the resulting tunnel.
A few bytes, then just copying
The SOCKS negotiation selected a method and opened the requested remote connection. Subsequent application bytes used that relay path without becoming SOCKS commands themselves.
The client opens a TCP connection to its configured SOCKS proxy. Application traffic waits until the proxy negotiation finishes.
Version 5, and how to log in
The client lists authentication methods it supports. The proxy selects one method or rejects the proposed choices.
A CONNECT request names the destination using an address or domain name and port. The proxy reports whether it established that remote connection.
After success, bytes pass through the proxy in both directions. Any application encryption is negotiated by the endpoints above this relay layer.
A reverse proxy is the public endpoint in front of an application server. Trace where TLS ends and how the proxy forwards requests to its backend.
The public and backend connections are separate conversations. Encryption on one hop does not automatically protect the other, so deployment boundaries determine the exposure.
The client reaches the service’s public address. That address belongs to the reverse proxy rather than the backend application process.
Offloading: the proxy does the TLS work
The proxy authenticates itself and terminates the client’s TLS session. It can now inspect the decrypted HTTP request.
Passed on to the app server
The proxy forwards the request over a separate backend connection. If that connection is plaintext, the backend network must be trusted or otherwise protected.
The application processes the request and returns its response. Its transport peer is the proxy, which may add routing or client-address metadata.
The proxy wraps the response in the client-facing TLS session. The browser sees one secure origin even though the backend used another connection.
TLS can end at the proxy, continue with a new backend TLS session, or pass through to the application. These choices change visibility, trust boundaries and operational responsibility.
WireGuard carries IP packets inside authenticated encrypted UDP messages. Follow its compact key handshake and distinguish an inner web packet from the outer tunnel transport.
Encrypted to the VPN, plain beyond it
The tunnel protected inner packets between its configured peers. Traffic beyond the remote peer still follows the routing and application-security rules of that network.
Peers are configured with identities and allowed address ranges. The configuration determines which destinations should enter the tunnel.
The peers exchange fresh ephemeral contributions and authenticate their identities. The resulting session keys protect subsequent transport messages.
The sender wraps an inner IP packet in a protected tunnel message. An outer UDP/IP header routes that message to the remote peer.
The remote peer verifies and decrypts the message before forwarding its inner packet. The public web server sees the forwarded connection rather than the encrypted tunnel packet.
The response follows the reverse route into the tunnel. The local peer removes the outer protection and delivers the inner response to the application.
A small authenticated keepalive can preserve a NAT mapping during idle periods. It maintains reachability without carrying application content.
IKEv2 negotiates security associations, and ESP protects the packets they carry. Follow NAT detection, authenticated key negotiation, and encapsulated traffic through an IPsec tunnel.
IKE to set up, ESP to carry
IKE established identities and keys while ESP carried the protected data. NAT traversal changed the outer transport without exposing the encrypted inner packet.
The peers propose cryptographic algorithms and exchange public key contributions. Fresh nonces help derive unique keys for this negotiation.
NAT detection reveals that addresses changed along the path. The peers can use UDP encapsulation so ESP traverses the mapping reliably.
An authenticated exchange proves the configured identities. It also installs the child security association used to protect application traffic.
An inner IP packet is encrypted and authenticated by ESP. Its outer headers route the tunnel message to the remote gateway.
Through the gateway and home again
The gateway decapsulates, forwards and protects the returning traffic. Separate sequence counters help reject replayed tunnel packets.
VPN protocols differ in negotiation, identity management and deployment requirements. The security boundary remains the pair of endpoints that decrypt the tunnel.
Modbus/TCP exposes device data and control operations as simple register and coil messages. Follow reads, writes and an exception, then examine the protocol’s lack of built-in access security.

The client read registers and wrote control values using request/reply transactions. Network placement and external security controls are critical because ordinary Modbus/TCP does not authenticate these operations.
A TCP connection to the PLC
The controller opens a TCP connection to the device’s Modbus service. The connection provides delivery, not proof that the client is authorized.
A read request names a starting register and a quantity. The response supplies consecutive 16-bit values in the requested range.
A write operation changes a selected register value. The reply confirms the addressed register and value, rather than granting an additional authorization check.
A coil write changes a boolean control output. The meaning of that bit depends on the device’s configured process model.
An unsupported address or operation produces an exception response. The function code’s high bit marks the error and the exception code explains it.
Classic Modbus/TCP has no application-layer encryption or identity check. A teaching network must distinguish protocol correctness from safe industrial access control.

Ethernet carries a frame across one local link. Follow a broadcast, watch a switch learn source addresses, then compare a local delivery with a frame sent to the router. IP identifies the destination host; MAC addresses identify the next link.
The switch only reads MAC addresses

The switch learned which ports lead to the laptop and desktop by reading source MAC addresses. Local frames stayed between those ports; the remote lookup used the router as its next hop. Old learned entries eventually expire so the table can follow changes.

The laptop can reach the desktop directly because both addresses share a subnet. It still needs the desktop’s MAC address, so ARP sends a broadcast. The switch copies that frame to the other ports and remembers where the laptop’s source MAC arrived.
Replies go to one port only

The desktop sends its MAC address back in a unicast reply. Reading the reply’s source teaches the switch that the desktop is on port 2. The destination is already known, so only the laptop’s port receives this reply.

The laptop now puts the desktop’s MAC address in an Ethernet header around its ping. The reply follows the same two ports in reverse. A learned unicast destination lets the switch avoid sending either frame to the router.

The resolver’s IP address is outside the home subnet, so the laptop hands this frame to its router. The Ethernet destination names that local next hop, while the IPv4 destination remains 8.8.8.8. The router’s MAC entry comes from an earlier ARP exchange that is outside this five-frame capture.

Learning is temporary: an address entry expires after a period with no traffic from that source. A later frame for an unknown destination is flooded until a source frame teaches the new port. This allows a moved device to be found again without editing a switch configuration.
